fixes.explanation: Ooh, nice guess, but the door is WIDER than that, friend. The LORD says, "…if a man or woman makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite…" (Numbers 6:2). Nothing in that verse says only priests can sign up. The priest does show up later to handle the offerings. He's more like the guy running the oven than the only one allowed to bake.

The basket is in this passage, so I see where you're coming from! But that basket is holding "…unleavened cakes made from fine flour mixed with oil…" (Numbers 6:15). Nobody is tossing hair in there. The hair goes "…on the fire under the peace offering." (Numbers 6:18). Hair in the cookie basket? Friend, that is a health inspector's nightmare.

Not quite, friend. It sounds sneaky-smart, but the text says he "…must not drink any grape juice or eat fresh grapes or raisins." (Numbers 6:3). Verse 4 goes further: nothing from the grapevine, "…not even the seeds or skins." So the raisin cookie is off the menu for him, and I feel for him on that one.

Right, it's False! Wine isn't the only thing on the list. The text says he "…must not drink any grape juice or eat fresh grapes or raisins." (Numbers 6:3). Then it adds that he's not to eat anything from the grapevine, "…not even the seeds or skins." (Numbers 6:4). The LORD covers the whole vine, top to bottom.

Yes, friend! "…no razor shall touch his head." (Numbers 6:5). For the entire period of the vow, the hair just grows. The text says he "…must let the hair of his head grow long." His barber is out of work for a while.

Good thought, but a comb isn't what the text names. It says "…no razor shall touch his head." (Numbers 6:5). The hair is to grow long for the whole vow. So the razor is the thing that stays far, far away.

A crown sounds fancy, I'll give you that! But the text says "…no razor shall touch his head." (Numbers 6:5). Nobody is putting on anything here. The hair is simply left alone to grow long for the whole vow.

Not quite, friend, and I think this one is a heavy line to read. The text says, "Even if his father or mother or brother or sister should die, he is not to defile himself…" (Numbers 6:7). There's no "just this once." Verse 7 gives the reason: the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head.

Right, it's False. I think this is one of the hardest lines in the passage. The text says, "Even if his father or mother or brother or sister should die, he is not to defile himself…" (Numbers 6:7). No exception is given for family. The reason is that the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head.

That's it, baker! The text says, "…because the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head." (Numbers 6:7). That's the reason it gives, even when the dead is family. His head carries the sign of his vow, so the LORD's "stay away" holds.

Good try, but hands and offerings aren't the reason given. The text says the Nazirite stays away "…because the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head." (Numbers 6:7). It's about his head. Hands are busy enough at my place without adding to the story.

I like the creativity, but there's no robe or tribe mark in this verse. The reason is "…because the symbol of consecration to his God is upon his head." (Numbers 6:7). It's all about the head, friend. Keep your eye on the head.

Yes, friend! If someone suddenly dies in his presence and defiles his consecrated hair, "…he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing…" (Numbers 6:9). That's the seventh day. All that growing, and the hair has to come off anyway. That's got to sting.

Washing clothes is a sensible guess, but this passage never mentions it here. The text says he "…must shave his head on the day of his cleansing…" (Numbers 6:9). The defiled thing is his consecrated hair, so the hair is what goes. The laundry can wait.

Oil is a nice thought, but this passage doesn't mention it for this moment. The text says he "…must shave his head on the day of his cleansing…" (Numbers 6:9). Consecrating his head again comes later, on that same day (Numbers 6:11). First the hair comes off, then the rest follows.

Seventh, that's right, baker! The text says the Nazirite must shave his head "…on the day of his cleansing…" and that is the seventh day (Numbers 6:9). Then comes the eighth day, when he brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest (Numbers 6:10). Seven days to cleanse, and then he's heading back to the Tent of Meeting.

Third is a solid guess, but the count is longer. The day of cleansing is the seventh day (Numbers 6:9). The eighth day is when he brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest (Numbers 6:10). So it's a full week, not three days.

Tenth is a little past it, friend. The text says the day of cleansing is the seventh day (Numbers 6:9). The very next day, the eighth, he brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest (Numbers 6:10). That's three days sooner than you picked.

True, and well done! The priest offers one bird as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, and then the text says, "On that day he must consecrate his head again." (Numbers 6:11). A fresh start for his head. The vow starts over, too.

Not quite, friend. It's True. After the priest offers the two birds, the text says, "On that day he must consecrate his head again." (Numbers 6:11). So he does rededicate it, and he doesn't skip that step.

That's right, baker! The text says, "But the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled." (Numbers 6:12). He rededicates his time of separation to the LORD and starts over. It's like a whole batch of dough dumped on the floor and the timer set back to zero.

Nice hope, but it doesn't go that way. The text says, "But the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled." (Numbers 6:12). He rededicates his time of separation to the LORD, so the new vow starts fresh. The old days stay behind.

Half credit sounds generous, friend, but the text doesn't say it. It says, "But the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled." (Numbers 6:12). None of them count. The new time of separation starts from the beginning.

Yes, the priest! The priest waves the shoulder, the cake and the wafer before the LORD, and the text says, "This is a holy portion for the priest…" (Numbers 6:20). The priest also gets the breast of the wave offering and the thigh that was presented. That's a nice spread.

Good thought, since the priest does put those items into the Nazirite's hands first (Numbers 6:19). But after the wave, the text says, "This is a holy portion for the priest…" (Numbers 6:20). So they end up as the priest's portion. The Nazirite gets to hold them, but not keep them.

The Levites are a fair guess, but they aren't mentioned in this passage. After the wave offering, the text says, "This is a holy portion for the priest…" (Numbers 6:20). It's the priest's portion, along with the breast and the thigh. Keep your eye on the priest.

True, baker, and it only took the whole vow to get here! The text says, "After that, the Nazirite may drink wine." (Numbers 6:20). That comes after the shave and the wave offering. The long separation is complete.
Not quite, friend. It's True. After the shave and the wave offering, the text says, "After that, the Nazirite may drink wine." (Numbers 6:20). The vow is finished, so the rule for it is finished too.

That's it, baker! The text says, "…he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation." (Numbers 6:21). If you make the promise, you keep it. It's as simple as saying you'll bring the cookies and then actually bringing the cookies.

Tempting when the days get long, I know! But the text says, "…he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation." (Numbers 6:21). There's no shortening it. He keeps it all the way through.

Nice try, but the vow isn't something he hands over. The text says, "…he must fulfill whatever vow he makes, according to the law of his separation." (Numbers 6:21). The priest helps with the offerings, but the vow belongs to the Nazirite. He's the one who has to see it through.
